procedural_history.originating_court: Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated October 26, 1969, of the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India in D.C. Appeal No. 18 of 1968, suspending the appellant from practice for a period of one year.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text mentions a case from the High Court of Bombay where an advocate was found guilty of misconduct, but no disciplinary action was taken. An appeal by special leave was sought, but the Judicial Committee did not advise granting it, primarily because it involved the High Court's discretionary decision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The case reached the Supreme Court via a special leave appeal under Section 38 of the Advocate's Act, 1961. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondent regarding the maintainability of the appeal, but it was rejected.

directions: The order of the Bar Council of India is set aside.
There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Advocate-General can be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and is therefore competent to file an appeal against an order of the disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council.

facts: A disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council made an order in a misconduct proceeding against an advocate.
The Advocate-General of the State, who had been given notice of the proceedings under Section 35(2) of the Advocates Act, disagreed with the committee's decision.
The Advocate-General filed an appeal to the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India.
The advocate argued that the appeal was incompetent because the Advocate-General was not a "person aggrieved" under Section 37 of the Act.
The Bar Council of India's committee rejected this argument, heard the appeal, found the advocate guilty, and suspended him from practice.
The advocate then appealed that decision to the Supreme Court, again raising the issue of the Advocate-General's competency to file the initial appeal.
law: Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, grants a right of appeal against an order of a State Bar Council's disciplinary committee to "any person aggrieved" by that order.
Section 35(2) of the Act requires that a disciplinary committee give notice of proceedings to the Advocate-General of the State, who has a right to be heard.

Generally, a "person aggrieved" is someone who has suffered a detriment, pecuniary or otherwise, or some form of prejudice due to an order. Merely having one's submissions rejected does not automatically make one an aggrieved person with a right to appeal.
application: The Supreme Court (by majority) analyzed the role of the Advocate-General in disciplinary proceedings.
The Court reasoned that the Advocate-General's function under the Act is to assist the disciplinary committee, not to be a party prosecuting the advocate.

Once the Advocate-General has appeared and made his submissions, his duty is fulfilled. The decision of the committee does not cause him any personal grievance or infringe upon any of his legal rights.
The Court held that the Advocate-General could not make the cause his own or act on behalf of others he did not represent.
Therefore, dissatisfaction with the committee's order does not place the Advocate-General in the category of a "person aggrieved" who has suffered a legal detriment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the Advocate-General is not a 'person aggrieved' within the meaning of Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961. As a result, the appeal filed by the Advocate-General to the Bar Council of India was incompetent.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Advocate-General can be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and is therefore competent to file an appeal against an order of the disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council.
appellant_arguments: The Advocate-General does not represent the public interest and therefore cannot be considered a 'person aggrieved' by an order of the Disciplinary Committee.

The provision in Section 35 of the Act, which entitles the Advocate-General to receive notice of the hearing, does not confer upon them the status of a 'person aggrieved' with the right to appeal under Section 37.
respondent_arguments: The Advocate-General is a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Act and is competent to file an appeal against the disciplinary committee's order.

The statutory requirement under Section 35(2) for the Advocate-General to be given notice and the right to appear in the proceedings implies they have a sufficient interest to appeal an adverse order.

cases.principle: The meaning of the expression 'person aggrieved' must be determined from the context of the specific statute in which it appears, rather than by importing definitions from decisions on similar expressions in different statutes.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A legal grievance must have a tendency to injure the person complaining; the mere fact that an order is wrong or acquits someone who the person believes should have been convicted does not, by itself, constitute a legal grievance.
obiter: An undefined expression must be construed by reference to the context of the enactment in which it appears and all the circumstances.
A decision in disciplinary matters is not a judgment of a court but is only deemed to be so by the legislature.
The court's conclusion does not mean it has gone into the merits of the advocate's plea, nor does it indicate how a judge would have decided the case on the facts.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Advocate-General cannot be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, merely because they disagree with a decision of a State Bar Council's disciplinary committee. The Advocate-General's personal opinion that a decision is erroneous, even if the matter is of public importance, does not constitute a legal grievance that confers a right to appeal. The statutory right to be heard in the proceedings does not automatically grant the status of a party with the right to appeal an adverse order.
legal_tests_applied: To qualify as a 'person aggrieved', the person must have a legal grievance, which is defined as having a tendency to injure them. The mere fact that an order is wrong or acquits someone who the person thinks ought to be convicted does not, by itself, give rise to a legal grievance.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the reasoning that the Advocate-General's role in maintaining professional standards and public interest automatically makes them an aggrieved person. The view that they are aggrieved when they find that the interests of the Bar and the public have not been properly safeguarded by a disciplinary committee's decision was not accepted by the majority.
why_respondent_won: A decision by the disciplinary committee does not become a matter of public interest merely because the Advocate-General feels it is erroneous; this is simply a personal opinion and its non-acceptance does not make him a person aggrieved.

An order that acquits someone the Advocate-General believes should be convicted does not by itself give rise to a legal grievance, as a legal grievance must have a tendency to injure the person appealing.
The Advocate-General's statutory right to appear at a hearing and make submissions does not confer the locus standi to file an appeal, as he is not a party to the proceedings.
The role of the Advocate-General is not that of a 'guardian angel of the Bar' or a 'champion of public interest' in every matter; their role is limited to what is specified in a given statute.
policy_considerations: The court established a clear policy on the limits of the Advocate-General's role in disciplinary matters, stating: 'An Advocate-General in India is not the guardian angel f the Bar, nor is he the champion of public interest in any matter save as specified in a statute.'
